# Appendix B: Answers to Review Questions

These are model answers to the review questions at the end of each chapter. They are
deliberately concise: each states the essential points and names the section where the
chapter develops them, so that you can check your own answer against the text and not just
against this page. Where a question asks for your own design, the answer shows what a strong
response contains; other well-reasoned designs are equally valid.

---

## Chapter 1 — Production AI Architecture

**1.** The system incorporates AI model inference as a critical-path component, so that if the
model fails or degrades the system cannot fulfill its core purpose; it is deployed to serve real
users or automate real business processes; it operates under defined service-level obligations,
SLAs or SLOs for availability, latency and quality; and it is a system, not a single model call,
including ingestion, orchestration, validation, caching, fallbacks, logging, monitoring and
integration with enterprise systems. (Section 1.1)

**2.** CLOSED is normal operation: calls pass through and failures are counted; when failures
exceed the threshold, the breaker moves to OPEN. In OPEN, every call fails immediately without
reaching the downstream service, giving it room to recover; after a timeout, the breaker moves to
HALF-OPEN. In HALF-OPEN, one test request is allowed: if it succeeds, the circuit closes and normal
operation resumes; if it fails, the breaker returns to OPEN for another timeout. (Section 1.3)

**3.** Queue-based load leveling. The API tier accepts each request immediately and places it on a
queue, returning a job ID; a worker tier consumes the queue at a rate the provider's limit allows,
about 500 requests per minute here, with retries and backoff on 429 responses; and clients poll for
results or receive them by webhook or WebSocket. The burst is absorbed by the queue instead of being
rejected; at 500 RPM, the last of 10,000 requests completes about 20 minutes later, so the design
must also set expectations or add capacity through a second provider or a higher limit, and
autoscale workers on queue depth within the rate limit. (Section 1.4)

**4.** Metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time, such as request counts, error rates
and latency histograms, and are the basis of dashboards and alerts. Traces follow one request
through every service and component it touches, showing where its time went and where it failed,
which is essential for diagnosing latency in multi-component pipelines. AI-specific metrics with no
traditional analog include tokens consumed per request, cost per request, the output-validation
pass rate, the fallback activation rate and context-window utilization. (Section 1.5)

**5.** Prompt injection, here indirect: instructions hidden in a user's document can override the
system prompt, for example to leak other users' data or the system prompt, or to trigger tool
actions. Countermeasures: keep system instructions and user content in separate message roles,
placing documents in a clearly delimited user or data section and never in the system prompt;
validate and sanitize inputs before they enter prompts; validate outputs to detect anomalous
behavior; scope retrieval and tools to the authenticated user, with least privilege and human
approval for irreversible actions. (Section 1.7)

**6.** Any three, argued for healthcare. LLM01 Prompt Injection: a patient's message or an uploaded
document could make the assistant ignore safety rules or disclose data. LLM02 Sensitive
Information Disclosure: the assistant could reveal protected health information from its context,
including other patients' records. LLM06 Excessive Agency: tools that book appointments, change
records or send messages must not act on adversarial input without validation and approval. LLM09
Misinformation is also especially relevant: a confident but wrong answer about symptoms or
medication can cause harm. (Section 1.7)

**7.** The context layer owns retrieval: it embeds queries with the right model version, scopes
results to the user's accessible documents, filters and scans for sensitive data, reranks, and
enforces the context budget. Calling the vector database directly from orchestration bypasses all
of that, so access control or PII scanning may be skipped, retrieval logic is duplicated and can
diverge, and orchestration becomes coupled to one vector store's API and schema, so changing the
store or the embedding model breaks code elsewhere. Working correctly today is not the test; the
hidden coupling reduces maintainability and makes the system's behavior harder to reason about.
(Section 1.10, Figure 1.4)

---

## Chapter 2 — AI System Design

**1.** A behavioral requirement specifies what the system produces for a given input; a quality
requirement specifies how good the AI output must be. For a resume screening service, a behavioral
requirement: "The system shall accept PDF and DOCX resumes up to 5 MB and return the extracted
skills, years of experience and a match score against the job description." A quality requirement:
"Skill extraction recall shall be at least 90% on the labeled validation set, and match scores
shall not differ significantly across groups defined by protected characteristics." (Section 2.1)

**2.** Orchestrator bloat is a single class or service that builds prompts, invokes tools,
validates output, caches, logs and applies business logic all at once. It is common because the
orchestrator touches every step of a request, so each new concern is easiest to add there, and the
component grows until it is very hard to test, debug or change safely. The principle that prevents
it is single responsibility: decompose the system into components, each with one clearly defined
job and its own contract, such as a prompt builder, an LLM client and an output validator, and
assign each requirement to exactly one component. (Section 2.3)

**3.** It is marginal. The components total 8,500 ms against a 10,000 ms SLO, a 15% margin, which
meets the chapter's minimum of 15–20% only at its lower edge. It is sound only if 8,000 ms is the
measured P95 of LLM inference at the expected output length, not a typical value; and it leaves no
room for a retry or a fallback to a second model on the synchronous path, either of which would
break the SLO. Strengthen it by measuring the LLM's P95, capping output tokens, using a faster model
or streaming, or moving long requests to the asynchronous pattern. (Section 2.7)

**4.** The client submits the request and immediately receives 202 Accepted with a job ID; the API
enqueues the job, and a worker processes it, persists the result and marks the job complete; the
client polls the job's status endpoint by ID, or receives a webhook, and retrieves the result. It is
preferred for long AI workloads because holding a synchronous connection open for many seconds
ties up server and client resources, runs into gateway, load-balancer and client timeouts, fails the
whole request if the connection drops, and cannot absorb load spikes; the asynchronous pattern
decouples acceptance from processing, so work can be queued, retried and scaled independently.
(Section 2.4, Figure 2.3)

**5.** At minimum: the specific action, for example "retry with a correction prompt that includes
the validation error"; its bound, such as at most two retries; what happens when the bound is
exhausted, such as a fallback model, a failed job state with a structured error to the caller, or
routing to human review; and how the failure is detected and monitored, such as a validation
failure metric and alert threshold. A good entry also names an owner. Without these, the mitigation
cannot be implemented or verified. (Section 2.8)

**6.** It prevents correct implementation, so it must be resolved before building begins. The
checklist requires error responses for every endpoint, and the contract is what client and server
teams build to: without a defined response for an unknown job ID, the server may return a 500 or
an empty 200, and clients will interpret it differently, retrying forever or treating the job as
lost. Fixing it after clients exist is a breaking change. Advisory findings improve the design but
do not stop it from being implemented correctly. (Section 2.9)

**7.** Data lineage documents, for each significant data entity, where it is created, modified,
stored and deleted. GDPR requires records of how personal data is processed, and lineage lets the
service answer what personal data it holds, where, for how long and why, and fulfil deletion
requests completely. For each entity, track the component that creates it, whether and where it is
modified, where it is stored, its retention period and how it is deleted; for example raw documents
in object storage deleted after a 24-hour TTL, prompts kept only as hashes in the audit log, and
results deleted on user request. A strong answer adds the purpose of processing and who has access.
(Section 2.5)

## Chapter 3 — Enterprise Workflows

**1.** In Human-in-the-Loop, a person reviews and approves the AI's output before it takes effect.
In Human-on-the-Loop, the AI acts automatically while a person monitors activity and can intervene,
with actions reversible within a window. HITL suits irreversible or high-stakes decisions, for
example a lawyer approving an AI-drafted contract amendment before it is sent. HOTL suits
high-volume, low-risk, reversible actions, for example AI responses to low-priority support tickets
that a supervisor samples and can recall within ten minutes. (Section 3.1)

**2.** Explicit legal transitions make the workflow's rules enforceable. If any transition were
allowed, a bug, race condition or malicious actor could move a document from pending review
straight to approved, skipping required review; reopen a completed item; or leave items in
impossible states that no process handles. Defining the allowed transitions, and rejecting all
others, guarantees that every item follows an approved path, that required approvals cannot be
skipped, and that the audit trail records only valid histories. (Section 3.7; Hands-on Lab)

**3.** When the 2-hour approval SLA expired, the SLA monitor should have moved the document to
`ESCALATED`, logged the escalation event with its reason, a timeout, reassigned it to a higher
authority, such as the approver's manager, with that level's own SLA, and notified both the
manager and the original approver. If the second level's SLA also expired before the 4-hour mark,
the document should have escalated again, to a director, and a timeout at the last level raises an
SLA breach alert, an incident record and manual resolution. The document should now be `ESCALATED`,
assigned at the second or third level, never still `PENDING_APPROVAL`; that it is still pending
means the escalation mechanism failed, which is itself an incident to investigate. (Sections 3.4,
3.9, Figure 3.3)

**4.** In the same database transaction as the state change, the workflow also writes an event
record to an outbox table; a separate process reads the outbox, delivers the events to downstream
systems, and marks them sent. It solves the dual-write problem: a state change and the
notification of it must both happen or neither. With a direct API call, the database commit can
succeed while the call fails or the process crashes, so the downstream system never learns of the
change; or the call succeeds and the commit fails, so it acts on a change that never happened. The
outbox records the event atomically with the state, so it cannot be lost; delivery is at-least-once,
so consumers must be idempotent. (Section 3.8, Figure 3.5)

**5.** Batch. No one is waiting for an immediate answer, the results are needed the next morning,
the volume is high and cost matters, which all favor batch processing, possibly with batch API
discounts. Architecturally, claims are collected during the day and processed in a scheduled
overnight run that must finish before morning with margin; the run must be resumable after
failures, with checkpointing, retries and a dead-letter path for failed items; it must respect rate
limits; and it ends with results stored and sorted for batch review, low-confidence classifications
first, with monitoring that alerts if the run will not complete in time. (Sections 3.1, 3.5, 3.6)

**6.** A high rejection rate means reviewers are rejecting many AI outputs, which signals a quality
problem: model drift, a changed input distribution, a prompt regression or a threshold set too
loosely. SLA compliance measures only whether items are resolved in time, so it can stay high while
the AI produces poor work that people catch and correct, at the cost of their time. If reviewers
start trusting the AI and rejecting less carefully, the same problem becomes errors that reach
customers. (Section 3.9)

**7.** A `WorkflowEvent` is an audit record of a state transition, written for accountability and
compliance: who moved which item from which state to which, when and why. A domain event published
to an event bus is a notification that something happened, such as `DocumentApproved`, written for
other systems to react to. They differ in audience, content, retention and guarantees: audit
records must be complete, immutable and retained, while domain events are designed for consumers
and may be filtered, transformed or expired. Neither replaces the other, though both can be written
in the same transaction, and the outbox pattern often does so. (Sections 3.7, 3.8)

---

## Chapter 4 — Automation

**1.** Rule-based automation executes fixed rules, if condition X then action Y: it is
deterministic and can be audited by inspecting its rules. AI-driven automation uses a learned or
generative model to decide which action an input calls for: it is probabilistic, so the same input
can occasionally produce a different result, and it must be governed with confidence thresholds,
validation and review. It provides value where rules cannot: when the decision cannot be expressed
as a finite set of explicit rules, when inputs are unstructured, such as natural language, images
and documents, when the decision must integrate many contextual signals, and when volume exceeds
what people can handle. (Section 4.1)

**2.** First, a confidence threshold model that sends low-confidence classifications to human
review instead of acting on them, so many of the 80 errors would have been caught before
processing, provided the thresholds are calibrated. Second, rollback: an action log that records
the before-state of every mutation, with actions reversible by design, so the incorrect actions can
be identified and reversed. Rate limits on consequential actions and anomaly detection on the
classification distribution would also have limited how far the failure spread before someone
noticed. (Sections 4.1, 4.8, 4.9)

**3.** Components communicate only through events: each finishes its work and publishes an event,
such as `WorkCompleted`, and the components that care subscribe and react; none calls another
directly. Decoupling improves resilience because a failing or slow consumer does not block the
producer or the other consumers; events can be buffered and retried, so a component can recover
and catch up; components can be deployed, scaled and changed independently; and new consumers can
be added without modifying existing ones. With direct calls, a failure in any callee propagates to
the caller and the whole chain fails. (Section 4.5; Mistake 3)

**4.** A self-healing system detects degraded or failed components and corrects them automatically,
without human intervention. Automated operation is the system doing its normal work, such as
classifying and routing documents; automated remediation acts on the system itself, restoring its
health when monitoring detects degradation, and it must be logged and alerted on so recurring
failures are not hidden. Appropriate conditions include transient LLM API failures, handled by retry
with backoff; sustained high error rates, handled by switching to a fallback model; worker crashes,
handled by restarting the worker; and queue buildup, handled by scaling up workers. (Section 4.6;
Mistake 4)

**5.** A real LLM API makes unit tests slow, costly, non-deterministic and dependent on network,
credentials and rate limits, so a failing test may say nothing about your code; and a unit test
should test one component in isolation. A mock makes the test fast, free and repeatable. It should
return deterministic, scripted responses in the same format as the real API: valid outputs for
each document category with defined confidence values, including values above, between and below
the routing thresholds, plus malformed output, empty responses, timeouts and errors, so each path in
the routing and error handling is exercised. (Section 4.7; Mistake 5)

**6.** A kill switch pauses or halts a pipeline without redeployment, typically a feature flag or
database record the pipeline checks before processing each item, so harm can be stopped
immediately. Activate it when the automation is causing or is likely to cause harm: a spike in
errors or rejected actions, a shift in the classification distribution, a runaway loop or volume
anomaly, a suspected security incident or manipulation, or a dependency behaving unexpectedly. The
chapter does not prescribe who may activate it; a sound policy lets the on-call engineer, the
pipeline's owner and the responsible risk or operations lead activate it at once, without approval,
because stopping must be easy, while restarting requires the owner's sign-off after the cause is
understood. Every activation is logged. (Section 4.9)

**7.** Deploy the new model alongside the current one with the pipeline in dry-run mode, so it
processes real inputs and records in the action log the actions it would take, without executing
them. Compare its intended actions with those the current model took on the same items:
agreement rate, the classification distribution, confidence distribution and the items where the
two disagree, which people review to judge which model was right. Activate the new model only if
it meets predefined criteria, then use a gradual rollout with the kill switch and rollback ready.
(Section 4.8)

---

## Chapter 5 — Model Deployment

**1.** A liveness probe checks whether the container is alive and responsive; if it fails
repeatedly, Kubernetes restarts the container, on the assumption that the process is stuck. A
readiness probe checks whether the container is ready to serve traffic, for example whether
startup has finished and dependencies are reachable; if it fails, Kubernetes removes the pod from
the Service's endpoints, so it receives no traffic, but does not restart it, and adds it back when
the probe passes. Readiness should therefore check dependencies, while liveness should not, or a
dependency outage would restart every pod. (Section 5.4; Hands-on Lab)

**2.** A multi-stage build installs and compiles dependencies in a builder stage and copies only
the runtime artifacts into a minimal final image. The security benefit is that compilers, build
tools, package caches and intermediate files are excluded from the image that runs, reducing the
attack surface and the number of packages that can carry vulnerabilities. The practical benefit is
a much smaller image, which pulls faster, starts faster and costs less to store and scan. (Section
5.3)

**3.** Roll back: route the canary's traffic back to the stable version and stop the rollout. A
3.1% error rate against 0.8% is almost four times the stable rate, well over the alert threshold of
two times stable and the automatic rollback trigger of two times baseline; continuing would expose
more users to errors. Mark the canary version retired with the reason, keep its logs, and hold a
post-incident review to find and fix the cause before trying again. (Sections 5.8, 5.10, Figure 5.5)

**4.** Anything in an image or a committed file is effectively published: everyone with access to
the registry or the repository can read it, image layers retain it even if a later layer deletes
it, version control keeps it in history forever, and it spreads to every copy, fork and backup,
where it cannot be revoked by deleting the file. Inject secrets at runtime: from a secrets manager
such as AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault, or Kubernetes Secrets, delivered as environment
variables or mounted files, with local `.env` files excluded through `.gitignore` and
`.dockerignore`. (Sections 5.3, 5.4; Mistake 1)

**5.** Record the new model identifier, which is tracked separately from the service version. For
the service version, it depends on whether the change reaches clients. If the different output
format changes the response schema clients depend on, it is a breaking change and increments
MAJOR, with API versioning so existing clients are not broken. If the service's validation and
normalization layer maps the new model's output back to the same response schema, the output
format is unchanged and it is a MINOR increment, the case the scheme defines as a new model with
the format unchanged. Either way, test the extraction outputs against the schema before deploying.
(Sections 5.6, 5.9)

**6.** Advantages: rollback is instant, a single DNS or load-balancer switch back to the old
environment, without redeploying; and the new version can be fully deployed and smoke-tested in a
production-identical environment before it receives any traffic, with no period in which old and
new versions serve traffic together. The primary cost is infrastructure: two full environments
must be maintained, roughly doubling infrastructure cost during deployment. (Sections 5.7, 5.8)

**7.** A shell smoke test needs only `curl`, available almost everywhere, so it can run from the
deployment pipeline, a bastion host or an operator's terminal against any environment, without
installing the Python test environment and its dependencies. It tests the deployed service from
the outside, over HTTP, as clients do, including networking, routing and configuration that unit
tests do not exercise; it is fast, so it suits the step that decides whether to switch traffic or
roll back; and it does not depend on the service's own code, so a broken dependency in the image
cannot hide a failure. The Python suite still runs in CI before deployment. (Section 5.7; Hands-on
Lab)

## Chapter 6 — Inference Optimization

**1.** Static batching pads every request to the longest one and finishes only when its slowest
member does: compute is spent on padding, and slots whose requests finish early sit idle until the
whole batch completes, while new requests wait for the next batch. Continuous batching schedules at
each generation step: a request that finishes is immediately replaced by a waiting one, so batch
slots stay filled with useful work and the GPU remains busy, instead of idling on padding and
finished sequences. (Section 6.3, Figure 6.2)

**2.** Any two. Use a stronger post-training quantization algorithm, such as GPTQ or AWQ, with a
calibration set representative of your own data instead of a naive rounding scheme. Use
quantization-aware training, which simulates quantization noise during fine-tuning so the model
learns to compensate, at the cost of a training run. Move to INT8, a middle ground that still
avoids FP16. Keep the most sensitive layers at higher precision in a mixed-precision scheme, or use
finer-grained, group-wise quantization scales. Re-measure on the team's own benchmark after each
change. (Section 6.4; Mistake 3)

**3.** It fails when the target model rarely accepts the draft's tokens, or when the target is not
the bottleneck. Examples: creative or high-temperature generation, or a draft model trained on a
different domain from the traffic, such as general text drafting for specialized legal output,
where acceptance rates are low and the drafting work is wasted; a draft model that is not much
smaller than the target, so drafting costs nearly as much as generating; a pipeline dominated by
network latency or post-processing, where faster decoding barely changes end-to-end time; and a
server already running large batches, where the GPU's spare compute that verification relies on
is used up. (Section 6.5)

**4.** An exact-match response cache first: with most traffic concentrated on 50 questions,
identical or near-identical queries recur constantly, and an exact-match cache, keyed on a hash of
the normalized query, serves them without any model call, at 100% precision, with no embedding
model and little implementation effort. Normalize whitespace and case so trivial variations still
match, set TTLs and invalidate on model or prompt changes. Add a carefully tuned semantic cache
later to capture paraphrases, since a loose threshold risks wrong answers; and pre-warm the cache
with answers to the 50 questions. (Sections 6.6, 8.3, 8.7)

**5.** Prefix caching works only on the replica that has the shared prefix's KV tensors in memory.
Round-robin sends consecutive requests with the same prefix to different replicas, so each replica
must compute and cache every prefix itself, cache hit rates fall roughly in proportion to the
number of replicas, and memory is wasted on duplicate entries. Use prefix-aware routing, for
example consistent hashing on the prefix or system-prompt identifier, so requests sharing a prefix
reach the same replica, combined with load awareness, such as least-connections, so one hot prefix
does not overload a single replica. (Sections 6.7, 6.9, Figure 6.4)

**6.** P99 latency is the value below which 99% of requests complete: the slowest 1% take longer.
The average hides the tail, because a few very slow requests barely move it, but those are what
users remember and abandon over; at scale, 1% of requests is many users every hour, and a user
whose session makes many requests is likely to hit the tail at least once. Interactive SLOs are
therefore set on tail percentiles. (Sections 6.10, 7.2; Mistake 4)

---

## Chapter 7 — Performance Engineering

**1.** An I/O-bound bottleneck. If the CPU were the constraint, utilization would be near 100%; at
15%, the process spends most of its 1,200 ms waiting, probably on network calls to the LLM API, a
database or an embedding service, likely made synchronously and one after another. Confirm with a
profiler, such as `py-spy`, which would show time spent blocked in network reads, and remedy it with
asynchronous I/O and concurrent calls, connection pooling and caching. (Section 7.4, Figure 7.1)

**2.** `asyncio` runs coroutines concurrently on a single thread with an event loop. When a coroutine
awaits a network response, it yields control to the loop, which runs other coroutines in the
meantime instead of blocking. `asyncio.gather()` starts all the independent calls together and waits
for all of them, so their waiting overlaps: total latency becomes roughly the slowest call, max(tᵢ),
instead of the sum, Σtᵢ. No threads are needed because the work is waiting, not computation, and
switching between coroutines is cheap. (Sections 7.7, 7.8)

**3.** Attention computation during prefill grows with the square of the sequence length, so halving
the prompt reduces it to (300/600)² = 1/4 of the original: a 75% reduction. The rest of prefill, the
linear projections and feed-forward layers, grows linearly and halves, so total prefill compute falls
by between 50% and 75%, closer to 75% for long prompts in which attention dominates. (Section 7.5)

**4.** A load test runs the system at expected peak traffic for a limited period, to verify that it
meets its latency and error targets under that load: run it before launches, before expected peaks
and after significant changes. A soak test runs the system at moderate load for many hours, to find
problems that appear only over time, such as memory leaks, connection-pool exhaustion, growing queues
and slow degradation: run it before a release that will run for a long time and after changes to
resource management. (Section 7.9)

**5.** Most requests are fast, but a minority are about 17 times slower: a long tail. It suggests that
some requests take a different, slow path or wait on something, for example cache misses against
hits, queueing when workers or rate limits are saturated, retries after timeouts or 429 responses,
long prompts or outputs, cold starts, garbage-collection pauses or a slow dependency. Investigate by
breaking down the slow requests by path, prompt size, cache status and time, using traces. (Sections
6.10, 7.2)

---

## Chapter 8 — Caching Strategies

**1.** Without the cache, 1,000 requests make 1,000 inference calls: 1,000 × $0.02 = $20.00. With a
40% hit rate, 400 are served from the cache and 600 call the model: 600 × $0.02 = $12.00, a saving
of $8.00, or 40%, before the cost of running the cache, which is usually small by comparison.
(Sections 8.1, 8.9)

**2.** Prompts can be thousands of tokens long, so raw keys waste memory and network bandwidth,
make lookups and comparisons slower, and can exceed key-size limits or degrade indexing in the cache
backend. Raw keys also store full prompt text, which may contain personal or sensitive data, in a
place often less protected than primary storage, and expose it in logs and monitoring tools. A
SHA-256 hash of the normalized prompt gives a fixed-size, uniformly distributed key. (Section 8.3)

**3.** Raise the threshold, toward the range the chapter describes as common, around 0.92–0.97, and
tune it on real query pairs labeled as equivalent or not, choosing the value that keeps false
matches acceptably rare. At 0.80, queries that share most of their words but differ in the detail
that decides the answer, such as a country, a date, a weight or an account, are treated as the
same question. Also require exact agreement on the entities that matter for the domain, and monitor
stale reads such as regenerations and negative ratings. (Sections 8.4, 8.9; Mistake 2)

**4.** When a popular cache entry expires, many simultaneous requests miss at once and all try to
recompute it, flooding the model or backend with identical expensive work and causing latency
spikes or outages. Probabilistic early expiration lets each request, before expiry, decide at random
whether to recompute the entry, with a probability that rises sharply as expiry approaches and with
how long recomputation takes. One request usually refreshes the entry slightly early while the others
keep receiving the cached value, so the entry never expires under load and requests do not
recompute it together. A lock is the deterministic alternative. (Section 8.7)

**5.** Before returning a cached answer, verify that the new query matches the cached one on every
clinically significant detail, such as the drug, dose, condition, age group, pregnancy and other
contraindications, exactly, not just by similarity; use a high threshold tuned on medical query
pairs; never serve personalized answers across users; check that the cached response was generated
with the current model, prompt and knowledge-base version and is within its TTL, invalidating it
when guidance changes; and for high-risk questions skip the cache or send answers for review. Log
which cached answer was served for each query, for audit. (Sections 8.4, 8.5; Mistake 3)

---

## Chapter 9 — Security

**1.** In direct injection, the attacker controls the user input and embeds instructions in it.
In indirect injection, the attacker plants instructions in external content, such as web pages,
documents, database records or emails, that the system later retrieves into its context; the
attacker never interacts with the system. Indirect injection is harder to defend against because
the payload arrives through trusted-looking data channels instead of the input boundary, may be
hidden from people, can wait in a data source until retrieved and affects any user whose request
retrieves it; and every data source becomes an attack surface. (Sections 9.3, 9.4)

**2.** HS256 signatures are verified with a shared secret, so anyone holding one valid token can run
an offline brute-force or dictionary attack, trying candidate secrets until one reproduces the
token's signature; an 8-character secret can be found quickly with commodity hardware. With the
secret, the attacker can forge tokens with any claims, such as another user's identity or an admin
role, and the server will accept them. Fix: use a cryptographically random secret of at least 256
bits, the size of the hash, stored in a secrets manager and rotated; or switch to an asymmetric
algorithm, RS256 or ES256, so only the issuer holds the signing key; and pin the accepted algorithms,
use short expiry times and invalidate all outstanding tokens after replacing the secret. (Sections
9.7, 9.8)

**3.** Ten, or eleven if the requests are spread across the whole second. The bucket starts full with
10 tokens, so the first 10 requests each consume one and succeed; at 1 token per second, about one
more token is added during the second, so a request arriving near its end may succeed as well. The
rest are rejected with HTTP 429. If all 15 arrive at once, exactly 10 succeed. (Section 9.9)

**4.** Input validation catches only known attack patterns and cannot catch indirect injection that
arrives through retrieved content, novel or obfuscated attacks, or failures that are not attacks at
all. The model can produce harmful output from benign input: leaking system prompt content or
sensitive data from its context, hallucinating, producing malformed output or policy-violating
content. Output validation is the last line of defense before the response reaches users or
downstream systems, checking schema conformance, system prompt content, sensitive patterns and
policy. Defense in depth assumes each layer will sometimes fail. (Sections 9.3, 9.10)

**5.** Any two. First, a RAG pipeline puts content retrieved from documents into the context on every
request, so anyone who can add or modify a document in the corpus, such as an uploaded file, a shared
wiki page or a crawled web page, can plant instructions that reach many users' contexts. Second,
retrieval selects documents by semantic similarity, so an attacker can craft a document to rank
highly for target queries and be retrieved exactly when wanted. Third, retrieved content often sits
in the context with an authoritative framing, as "relevant knowledge," which encourages the model to
follow it, and combined with tools it can trigger exfiltration. A plain chatbot sees only the user's
own messages. (Section 9.4; OWASP LLM08)

**6.** LLM07, System Prompt Leakage, in the 2025 OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. The attack is
usually carried out through prompt injection, LLM01, and the defense is to keep secrets out of system
prompts, assume they can leak, and filter outputs that resemble system prompt content. (Sections 9.1,
9.5)

---

## Chapter 10 — Privacy

**1.** The core issue is the processor relationship under Article 28. A provider that processes
your users' personal data must do so only on your documented instructions, as your processor
under a data processing agreement; using it to improve its own models is processing for its own
purpose, which makes it a controller for that processing (Article 28(10)), needs its own lawful
basis, and conflicts with purpose limitation (Article 5(1)(b)), since the data was collected to
provide your service. Action: do not send personal data under those terms; use the provider's
business or API terms that exclude training on customer data, or opt out, with a DPA in place; if
that is impossible, choose another provider or redact personal data before it is sent; and record
the decision in your records of processing and DPIA. Confirm the analysis with counsel. (Sections
10.4, 10.7)

**2.** In an AI system, personal data spreads beyond the relational database: into logs, including
prompt and conversation logs; into embeddings in vector databases; into caches of responses and
embeddings; into backups; into data shared with providers; and possibly into training data and
model weights, from which it cannot practically be removed without retraining. Deleting only the
database rows leaves these copies, so the user's data remains processed and retrievable. Erasure
must cover every store, with identifiers on every record so copies can be found, and the deletion
must itself be logged. (Section 10.6; Mistake 3)

**3.** Any two. Prompt minimization strips personal data the task does not need, such as names and
emails from a ticket to be summarized, so it is never transmitted to the provider, logged or
retained, which removes exposure at the source. Query abstraction replaces specifics with
generalizations, such as "a 40-year-old patient with Type 2 diabetes" in place of a named patient
with a date of birth, so the model can still answer while the data sent no longer identifies the
person. Both reduce the harm of a breach, a provider incident or a log leak, and reduce legal
obligations, because data that is not processed cannot be exposed. (Section 10.4)

**4.** A false positive: a value with the same shape that is not an SSN, such as a part number or
reference "Ref 123-45-6789"; the unanchored pattern also matches inside longer digit runs, such as
"234-56-7890" within "1234-56-78901," and accepts numbers that cannot be valid SSNs, such as those
beginning with 000, 666 or 9. A false negative: an SSN written without dashes, "123456789," with
spaces, "123 45 6789," or with other separators such as en dashes. Fixes include word boundaries,
validity rules and context words such as "SSN," with NER as a second layer. (Section 10.3)

**5.** Verify the requester's identity and locate all their data, using the user identifier
stored as metadata with every record. Delete the conversation embeddings from the vector database
by that identifier, and delete the source conversations, logs, caches of responses and embeddings,
and derived records. Instruct service providers and contractors, including the AI provider, to
delete the data they hold. Handle backups by deleting from them or by ensuring that deleted data
expires with the backups and is suppressed if a backup is restored. Retain only what an exception
requires, such as legal obligations, and keep a log that the deletion occurred, without the deleted
content. Respond within 45 days, and confirm completion to the consumer. (Sections 10.6, 10.8)

---

## Chapter 11 — Governance

**1.** A Model Card documents an individual model: its details, intended use, factors, metrics,
evaluation and training data, disaggregated performance, ethical considerations and caveats. A
System Card documents a deployed application or service: its architecture, which models, tools
and data sources it uses, its deployment context and user population, safety evaluations,
safeguards, operational policies, monitoring and known limitations. For example, a model card
reports performance disaggregated by language on evaluation datasets; a system card reports that
outputs pass a moderation classifier and that refunds over a threshold require human approval,
information that belongs to the system, not the model. (Sections 11.3, 11.4)

**2.** High-risk: AI systems used in employment for recruitment or selection, including screening
or filtering applications, are listed as high-risk under the Act. The provider must operate a risk
management system and data governance, prepare technical documentation, enable automatic logging,
provide transparency and instructions for use, build in human oversight, meet accuracy, robustness
and cybersecurity requirements, run a quality management system, complete a conformity assessment
and register the system in the EU database. The company deploying it must use it according to the
instructions, assign competent human oversight, monitor its operation, keep the logs for at least
six months, and inform workers' representatives, affected workers and the candidates subject to its
decisions. GDPR Article 22 also applies to decisions based solely on automated processing. Check
which obligations apply on your dates, since they phase in, and confirm with counsel. (Section
11.2; Chapter 12, Section 12.3; Chapter 10, Section 10.7)

**3.** A user report activates T2, operational: the on-call engineer reviews within four hours,
confirming what was said, blocking or mitigating the behavior and logging the incident. Medical
advice from a system not designed for it also carries potential legal and regulatory exposure, so
it should be escalated to T4, involving legal, compliance and leadership, within two hours; and if
review finds a systematic pattern, T3, product and engineering, investigates the cause within 24
hours. Follow-up actions: preserve the conversation and logs; check how often it has happened;
strengthen the safeguards, such as output classification for medical content and clearer refusals;
update the system card's known limitations; notify affected users if harm is possible; and write an
incident report. (Section 11.7)

**4.** Governance consists of decisions and controls actually applied; a document that no one reads
does not change what is built or deployed, so its risks go unmanaged while the organization
believes it is covered. Two mechanisms: make documentation a gate in the workflow, so a deployment
cannot proceed until the model card, system card and assessments are current and reviewed, for
example a CI/CD check or a required review-board approval; and assign each document an owner and an
update cadence, linked to events such as each model version, with periodic audits and incident
reviews that check the documentation against reality. (Sections 11.8, 11.9; Mistake 1)

**5.** "Well" is not measurable or comparable: it names no metric, no value, no dataset, no
comparison with other groups and no uncertainty, so no one can check it or decide whether the model
is fit for a use. Replace it with disaggregated quantitative analysis: the specific metric, such as
accuracy, false-positive rate or recall, for group X and for the other groups, on a named evaluation
dataset, with sample sizes and confidence intervals, the gap between groups, and the threshold that
counts as acceptable. (Section 11.3)

**6.** A model risk committee, in regulated industries such as finance and healthcare, is a formal
body that reviews model validation results and approves models for production, as part of model
risk management under requirements such as SR 11-7: it ensures models are independently validated,
monitored and periodically reviewed, and that model risk is controlled. An AI ethics board is a
cross-functional committee, including technical, legal, ethics, product and external perspectives,
that reviews high-risk deployments for broader ethical and societal concerns, investigates
significant incidents and maintains policy. The first is a regulatory control focused on model
soundness and performance; the second addresses whether and how a system should be deployed at
all. (Section 11.8; Chapter 12, Section 12.6)

---

## Chapter 12 — Compliance

**1.** The Act classifies AI systems into four tiers. Unacceptable-risk practices, such as social
scoring and manipulative techniques, are prohibited. High-risk systems, in areas such as critical
infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services, law enforcement, migration
and justice, require conformity assessment, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human
oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and registration. Limited-risk systems have
transparency obligations, such as disclosing that a chatbot is an AI. Minimal-risk systems have no
mandatory obligations. A high-risk LLM application: an LLM system that screens job applications and
ranks candidates, or one that assesses applicants' creditworthiness from their documents. (Section
12.3)

**2.** GOVERN establishes policies, roles, accountability and culture: assign a named owner for the
chatbot and adopt a policy for incident handling. MAP establishes the context and risks: document
the chatbot's purpose, users, out-of-scope uses and potential harms, such as wrong policy answers.
MEASURE assesses and tests the risks: evaluate answer accuracy and harmful-output rates before
launch and in production, including adversarial testing for prompt injection. MANAGE prioritizes
and responds to them: implement safeguards such as output filtering and escalation to people,
monitor continuously, and maintain an incident response plan. (Section 12.4)

**3.** A model card documents one model, its intended use, performance, disaggregated evaluation,
training data and limitations; a system card documents the whole deployed system, model, prompts,
orchestration, safeguards, oversight and deployment environment. No regulation requires either by
name; they are standard formats for meeting documentation obligations. Model-card content supports
model-level requirements: the EU AI Act's documentation and information duties for providers of
general-purpose AI models, and SR 11-7's documentation of model purpose, limitations and
assumptions. System-card content supports system-level requirements: the EU AI Act's technical
documentation for high-risk systems (Annex IV), which covers the system and its human oversight,
and the NIST AI RMF's documentation of context, risks and limitations. (Sections 12.3, 12.6, 12.9;
Chapter 11, Sections 11.3, 11.4)

**4.** Audit logs are evidence: regulators, auditors and incident investigators rely on them to
reconstruct what the system did, and if they can be altered, by an attacker covering tracks or an
insider hiding an error, they prove nothing. Immutability also protects the organization, because
it can demonstrate that its records are complete. Two mechanisms: write-once storage, such as
object storage with a retention lock in compliance mode, for example S3 Object Lock, so no one can
modify or delete entries before the retention period ends; and cryptographic hash chaining, in which
each entry includes the hash of the previous one, so any modification is detectable. Both should be
combined with separation of permissions, so operational accounts can append but not modify or
delete. (Section 12.8)

**5.** Any three from at least two frameworks. EU AI Act: creditworthiness assessment is high-risk,
requiring conformity assessment, technical documentation, logging and human oversight; satisfied
technically with automatic decision logs retained for the required period, versioned documentation
generated from the model registry, and a review interface through which an officer can override
decisions. SR 11-7: independent validation before production and ongoing monitoring; satisfied with
a validation pipeline run by a separate team, performance and drift monitoring, and an annual
review recorded in the registry. Fair lending laws, such as ECOA: no discriminatory decisions;
satisfied with disparate-impact testing across protected classes before deployment and in
production, and with the ability to give applicants the specific reasons for adverse decisions.
GDPR Article 22, for EU applicants, adds the right to human intervention. (Sections 12.3, 12.6;
Chapter 10, Section 10.7)

**6.** An AI impact assessment evaluates the potential effects of an AI system on the people and
groups it affects and on society: harms such as discrimination, privacy intrusion, unsafe or
misleading outputs, effects on rights, and how they are mitigated. ISO/IEC 42001 requires such
assessments to be documented. A traditional software risk assessment focuses mainly on risks to the
organization and its systems, such as security, availability, project and operational risks. The
impact assessment looks outward at affected individuals, considers probabilistic and emergent
behavior and the data that shaped the model, and must be repeated as models, prompts and data
change. (Sections 12.1, 12.5, 12.9)

---

## Chapter 13 — Monitoring

**1.** Traditional monitoring checks availability and performance: is the system up, and is it fast?
AI systems add behavior. Identical-looking requests can produce materially different responses, and
behavior changes over time as the provider updates the model, the query distribution shifts, the
knowledge base is refreshed and the world changes; so a system with perfect uptime and latency can
fail silently at its core function. Standard infrastructure monitoring would miss quality
degradation, such as gradually less accurate or less helpful answers; behavioral drift, such as
changes in response length, tone or refusal rate after a model update; and safety and fairness
failures, such as successful prompt injections, harmful outputs or growing demographic disparities.
Cost explosions from token usage are a fourth. (Section 13.1)

**2.** Availability: uptime or health-check success; a drop means the service or a dependency is down.
Infrastructure: GPU memory or queue depth; growth indicates capacity shortage, fragmentation or a
slow consumer. Application: p99 latency or error rate; a rise indicates slow dependencies,
saturation or failing requests. AI-specific: the response quality score or safety filter rate; a
falling quality score indicates model, prompt or data drift, and a rising safety filter rate may
indicate adversarial activity or a model change. (Sections 13.2–13.5, Figure 13.1)

**3.** Model drift is the degradation of an AI system's behavior over time relative to its
baseline. Data drift is a shift in the inputs: the distribution of queries moves away from what the
system was designed and tested for, for example a support assistant tuned on formal business
questions starting to receive casual messages, or questions about a new product line. Concept drift
is a change in the correct answer for a given kind of query, for example a returns policy or price
list that changes, so answers that were right become wrong. For hosted models, a provider's model
update is a third source. (Section 13.9)

**4.** PSI = Σᵢ (Actualᵢ − Expectedᵢ) × ln(Actualᵢ / Expectedᵢ), summed over the bins of a
distribution, where Expectedᵢ is the proportion of the baseline in bin i and Actualᵢ the proportion
in the current period. Below 0.1 there is no significant drift; 0.1 to 0.25 is moderate drift to
investigate; 0.25 or more is significant drift that calls for revalidation. To apply it to quality
scores, take a baseline period of known-good scores, define bins on it, for example ten deciles;
compute the share of each period's scores, for example each day's, in each bin; add a small
constant to empty bins so the logarithm is defined; compute PSI daily and alert at the thresholds.
PSI detects a change in shape, not direction, so look also at whether the mean fell. (Section 13.9,
Figure 13.3)

**5.** Meaning: the automated quality score has stayed below 0.65 for 30 minutes, so users are
probably receiving poor answers. Verify: check that the evaluator itself is working, since a broken
judge or scoring service produces low scores; sample and read affected responses; check whether
the drop affects all traffic or one prompt template, topic, model version or customer segment.
Diagnose: look for recent changes, such as prompt deployments, model or provider updates,
knowledge-base refreshes, retrieval errors or a traffic shift, using grouping by template and model
version in the logs. Mitigate: roll back the recent prompt or model change; pin the previous model
version; switch to the fallback model; disable the failing feature or route affected requests to
people. Escalate: if no cause is found and mitigated within the response time for its severity, or
if the drop affects safety, compliance or a large fraction of users, escalate to the service owner
and incident commander, and to legal or compliance if harmful outputs may have reached users.
Afterwards, hold a post-incident review. (Sections 13.6, 13.8, 13.10)

**6.** Quality metrics are noisy from minute to minute and degrade gradually. A single point-in-time
threshold either fires on momentary blips, causing alert fatigue, or, set loosely enough to avoid
them, misses slow declines. A short window catches acute incidents quickly; a long window catches
gradual drift that no short window shows; and requiring both to agree before paging filters out
brief spikes while still reacting quickly to a real, sustained change. (Section 13.6)

---

## Chapter 14 — Evaluation

**1.** Reference-based evaluation compares output with a ground-truth answer; reference-free
evaluation judges quality without one, by criteria such as factual consistency with the context,
relevance or a rubric. Reference-based suits tasks with well-defined correct outputs, for example a
regression suite of extraction tasks with known field values, where a reference makes scoring
exact and cheap and reference-free judgment would add cost and noise. Reference-free suits open-ended
production traffic, for example a support assistant's answers to live questions, where many responses
are correct and no reference exists, so a reference-based metric is impossible or would penalize
valid answers. (Sections 14.2–14.4; Mistake 3)

**2.** A strong language model, the judge, evaluates another model's outputs against a rubric,
giving scalable judgments that can approach those of human experts once calibrated. Position bias:
judges prefer the first of two responses; randomize order and average both orderings. Verbosity bias:
judges rate longer responses higher; include explicit conciseness criteria and, where possible,
compare responses of similar length. Self-preference bias: a model favors its own outputs or
similar ones; use a judge from a different model family. Above all, calibrate the judge against
human ratings before relying on it, and recheck periodically. (Section 14.5; Mistake 2)

**3.** BLEU measures n-gram precision against references, with a brevity penalty, and is the
standard for machine translation. ROUGE measures recall of reference n-grams, or with ROUGE-L the
longest common subsequence, and is the standard for summarization. BERTScore compares contextual
token embeddings between output and reference, and suits tasks in which paraphrase matters, such as
abstractive summaries or open answers with a reference. BLEU and ROUGE both depend on exact surface
overlap, so they penalize valid paraphrases and synonyms; BERTScore captures semantic equivalence
through embeddings. (Section 14.3)

**4.** Triggers: every change to prompts, models, retrieval configuration or the knowledge base, run
before deployment; a scheduled run, for example nightly, to detect provider-side changes; and
continuous sampling of production traffic. Dimensions: retrieval quality, as context recall and
precision on a labeled set; faithfulness to retrieved context; answer relevance; correctness on
questions with reference answers; safety and policy compliance; and latency and cost. Quality gates:
block deployment if any dimension falls below the range the unchanged system produces on repeated
runs, or below absolute minimums for faithfulness and safety, applied per slice such as topic,
language and customer tier as well as overall. Alerting: in production, page when faithfulness or
quality scores fall below their thresholds in both a short and a long window, for example sustained
over 30 minutes and over six hours; alert at lower severity on gradual decline or drift in the
question distribution. Calibrate the judge with human review on a small sample, and refresh the
evaluation set from production. (Sections 14.7, 14.8; Chapter 13, Section 13.6)

**5.** Randomization unit: the user or session, assigned by hashing its ID, so each user sees one
variant consistently. Sample size: choose the primary metric, for example task resolution or a
calibrated quality score, and the minimum detectable effect worth deploying; estimate the metric's
variance from historical data; and compute the sample size for the chosen significance level and
power, fixed before the test starts. Duration: long enough to reach that sample and to cover weekly
cycles, at least one week. Guardrail metrics: safety filter rate, escalation and complaint rates,
latency and cost per request, which must not degrade. Analysis: a two-sample t-test or confidence
interval for continuous scores and a chi-squared test for rates, analyzed per user, since requests
from the same user are not independent; report the effect size with its confidence interval, check
the guardrails and key segments, and do not stop early because the result looks significant.
(Section 14.9; Mistake 4; Volume II, Chapter 13)

**6.** Inter-rater reliability measures how consistently annotators agree, with statistics such as
Cohen's kappa for two annotators with categorical labels and Krippendorff's alpha for more annotators
or ordinal scales. It is essential because human labels are the reference standard used to
calibrate automated metrics: if annotators disagree, the labels measure the annotators rather than
the outputs, and anything calibrated on them inherits the noise. If two annotators consistently
disagree on "helpfulness," the definition is the problem: replace it with operationalized,
observable criteria, such as "answers the question directly, with no missing information, and gives
a next step," add anchored examples for each rating, run both annotators through a calibration set,
discuss and adjudicate the disagreements, revise the guidelines, and re-measure agreement before
labeling continues; split the dimension if it bundles two different things. (Section 14.6)

---

## Chapter 15 — Cost Optimization

**1.** Input tokens are processed together in one parallel prefill pass, which uses the GPU's
compute efficiently. Output tokens are generated one at a time, each needing its own forward pass
that reloads the model's weights and reads a growing KV cache, while the request holds GPU memory
throughout; per token, generation therefore uses far more of the provider's capacity, and pricing
reflects it, at five times the input price for GPT-6.1 Sol at the time of writing. For design, output
length is the most expensive dimension to leave unconstrained: ask for concise answers, constrain
format and length, set output-token limits as a safety net, and prefer structured outputs to
verbose prose. (Sections 15.1, 15.2; Chapter 6, Sections 6.1, 6.3)

**2.** Input: 5,000,000 × 500 = 2.5 billion tokens = 2,500 × $2.00 = $5,000. Output:
5,000,000 × 250 = 1.25 billion tokens = 1,250 × $10.00 = $12,500. Monthly cost: $17,500. Reducing
input tokens by 20% saves 20% of the input cost, $1,000 a month, bringing the total to $16,500. The
saving is modest because output tokens are nearly three-quarters of the cost; shortening outputs by
the same share would save two and a half times as much. (Section 15.2)

**3.** Embed the incoming query; search the cache for the nearest stored query embedding; if it is
within the similarity threshold and the cached entry is still valid, return the cached response;
otherwise call the model, store the embedding and response, and return the new response. The key
parameter is the similarity threshold, or distance threshold δ: loosening it raises the hit rate
but returns answers to questions that differ in ways that matter; tightening it protects quality
but lowers the hit rate. Tune it on real pairs of queries labeled as equivalent or not, choose the
loosest value whose false-match rate is acceptable, set it per risk category, require exact
agreement on key entities, and monitor stale serves and regenerations in production. (Section 15.7;
Chapter 8, Section 8.4)

**4.** A router classifies each request, for example with rules plus a small classifier, and sends
it to a tier, with a quality check that can escalate. (a) FAQ lookups: a small, fast model such as
GPT-6 Luna, grounded in retrieved FAQ content and backed by exact and semantic caches; answers are
short and well defined, so a premium model adds cost without quality. (b) Complaint handling: a
medium or premium model, because tone, empathy and judgment matter and a poor response risks the
customer relationship; the risk is moderate to high even when the reasoning is simple, with escalation
to a person for refunds or legal threats. (c) Technical troubleshooting: the best available model, or
a reasoning model, because the task needs multi-step reasoning, and an error wastes the customer's
time and generates further contacts. Measure quality per route with the evaluation suite and adjust
the routing from the data. (Sections 15.4, 15.6, Figure 15.3)

**5.** Showback reports each team's consumption without charging them; hard chargeback bills actual
AI costs against team budgets. Showback suits early adoption, or organizations where AI use should be
encouraged: it builds awareness of cost without discouraging experimentation, though teams have no
direct reason to economize. Hard chargeback suits mature, large-scale use with established budgeting
processes: it gives strong incentives to optimize prompts and choose cheaper models, but can
discourage valuable experimentation and needs fair attribution and budget allocation. Soft chargeback
is the middle ground. (Section 15.10)

**6.** The cascade sends every request first to the cheap model; a quality check evaluates the
result, and requests that fail are retried on the expensive model. Let the expensive model's cost be
1 and the cheap model's c. Every request pays c, and a fraction Pₑ also pays 1, so the expected cost
is c + Pₑ, relative to 1 for sending everything to the expensive model. The average cost reduction is
1 − (c + Pₑ). With c = 0.1 and Pₑ = 0.15, the cost is 0.25 and the reduction 75%. The cascade saves
money only when c + Pₑ < 1, ignoring the cost of the quality check, and escalated requests take two
model calls of latency; a check that misses the cheap model's failures saves money by shipping worse
answers. (Section 15.6)

---

## Chapter 16 — Scalability

**1.** By Little's Law, the average number of requests in the system equals the arrival rate times
the time each spends in it: L = λW = 100 requests per second × 5 seconds = 500 requests in flight at
any moment. Every component on the request path must hold 500 concurrent requests, with headroom:
the load balancer and API gateway connection limits and timeouts; the number of service instances
and their workers or async event loops; connection pools to the LLM API, databases and caches;
memory for in-flight request buffers; file descriptors and sockets; and the provider's rate limits,
in requests and tokens per minute. (Section 16.1; Chapter 6, Section 6.2)

**2.** Reactive, CPU-based autoscaling adds instances when CPU or memory utilization passes a
threshold, responding to resource use that has already risen. For services that call hosted
models, CPU stays low while requests wait on the API, so CPU is a poor signal of load. Proactive,
queue-depth-based scaling adds instances or workers when waiting work accumulates, or when latency
or concurrency approaches limits, so it tracks the real load before latency degrades. Use CPU-based
scaling for CPU-bound work, such as local embedding computation or self-hosted inference where
utilization tracks load; use queue depth and concurrency for I/O-bound services calling hosted
models and for queue-based workers, scaling within the provider's rate limits. (Section 16.5)

**3.** Sticky sessions route all of a user's requests to one worker, so load cannot be balanced
evenly, especially when request durations vary; rolling deployments and scale-in must wait for
sessions to end or break them; and when a worker fails, its users' sessions are lost, making each
worker a single point of failure. Instead, externalize state: keep session context, agent state
and rate-limit counters in a shared store such as Redis, with TTLs, or a database, so any worker can
handle any request. The trade-offs are a network round trip to load and save state on every request,
the cost and operation of the store, which must itself be highly available and scaled, and handling
concurrent updates to the same session. (Sections 16.2, 16.8)

**4.** Round-robin sends each request to the next instance in turn, ignoring how busy it is;
least-connections routes to the instance with the fewest in-flight requests. With latencies from 1 to
30 seconds, round-robin can pile several long requests onto one instance while others sit idle,
creating hot spots and long queues; least-connections accounts for work in progress, because an
instance busy with long requests has more open connections and receives fewer new ones. Choose
least-connections, or better, least outstanding requests weighted by estimated cost, such as context
length. (Section 16.4)

**5.** Use a token bucket per tenant, stored in Redis for consistency across instances, at two
granularities: a daily quota, 50 requests for Free and 1,000 for Standard, and a per-minute rate to
prevent bursts that exhaust shared capacity, for example 5 per minute for Free and 60 for Standard,
plus a token-based limit, since request costs vary widely. Track per tenant and per user within each
tenant, so one user cannot use a tenant's whole quota. "Unlimited" Enterprise means no daily quota,
not no protection: give each Enterprise tenant a large bucket, sized to its contract, for bursts, a
sustained refill rate within the platform's provider capacity, a priority queue, so excess requests
wait instead of failing, and alerts on unusual spikes. Return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header and
the remaining quota in response headers when a limit is exceeded, and keep a global limit protecting
the upstream API. (Sections 16.6, 16.7; Chapter 9, Section 9.9)

**6.** An LLM call takes one to ten seconds, while the network round trip to a distant region is tens
of milliseconds to a few hundred, a small fraction of the total; routing users to a nearer region
therefore changes end-to-end latency very little, unless the model API also has faster regional
endpoints, although time to first token with streaming is worth measuring. The primary benefits of
global deployment are compliance, keeping personal data, model calls and audit logs in the region
required by data-protection law or contracts, and resilience, failing over when a region or its model
API is degraded. (Section 16.10)

---

## Chapter 17 — Future Enterprise AI

**1.** Distillation, quantization and mixture-of-experts reduce the compute and memory per unit of
capability, so each generation of capability becomes cheaper to run, and capabilities that now need
a frontier hosted API are likely to run on smaller models, on-premises or on devices. For investment
strategy this means that building a competitive advantage on access to today's frontier capabilities
is temporary: they become commodity. Invest instead in what lasts: proprietary data and context,
evaluation capability, AI-native processes and the judgment to use AI well; avoid long commitments
tied to one model's current price or limits; and design systems so models can be swapped as cheaper,
better ones arrive. (Sections 17.1, 17.5)

**2.** L0 reactive: single-turn answers with no memory. L1 context-aware: multi-turn with session
memory. L2 tool-using: executes tools to gather information, such as RAG with function calling. L3
planning: decomposes goals and executes multi-step plans, as ReAct agents do. L4 self-correcting:
evaluates its outputs and revises plans on failure. L5 collaborative: multiple specialized agents
coordinating. L6 autonomous: persistent agents pursuing long-horizon goals. Most production enterprise
systems operate at the lower and middle levels, typically L1 to L3, with higher levels in bounded,
well-instrumented domains. Moving from L3 to L5 requires shifting oversight from reviewing each
output to defining goals, limits and exceptions; stronger error detection and recovery, because
mistakes compound; audit trails able to reconstruct multi-agent reasoning; and accountability
structures that assign clear owners for outcomes produced by chains of agent decisions. (Section
17.3; Mistake 2)

**3.** Sovereign AI means developing and operating AI infrastructure within a jurisdiction, reducing
dependence on foreign providers and keeping data under local control. Its drivers are data
sovereignty, strategic autonomy, economic competitiveness and regulatory compliance. For a European
healthcare company, the architecture requires inference on-premises or in a sovereign cloud located
in the EU and operated by entities subject to EU law; patient data, logs, embeddings and any
fine-tuning data processed and stored in the EU; GDPR controls for special-category health data,
with DPIAs, access control and audit; and no transfer of patient data to foreign-operated APIs.
Open-weight models that can be self-hosted include the Llama, Mistral and Falcon families; check each
license, since not all are open source in the strict sense, and evaluate them on the company's
clinical and language tasks. (Section 17.6; Chapter 10, Section 10.7)

**4.** As tool, the person initiates and the AI executes specific tasks on demand, with the person
retaining full control. As assistant, the AI proactively surfaces information, suggestions and
warnings, and the person reviews and decides. As colleague, AI and person work in parallel on
complementary parts of a task, the AI researching, drafting and analyzing, the person exercising
judgment and accountability. As delegate, the person defines goals and the AI executes autonomously
within boundaries, with the person reviewing outcomes. For contract review today, assistant is the
most appropriate: the AI flags non-standard clauses, missing terms and risks, and suggests language,
while lawyers decide, because legal judgment and accountability must stay with them and AI errors in
legal interpretation are costly; for high-volume, standardized documents, a bounded colleague model
can be justified once evaluation shows it reliable. (Section 17.8)

**5.** The maturity table shows that Stage 3 requires systematic evaluation, a full governance
framework, governed data and a platform engineering capability. In order: first, systematic
evaluation of the customer-service deployment, with a labeled evaluation set, quality metrics, and a
measured baseline, because the 30% figure and every later decision depend on measurement, and
anecdotal evaluation cannot show whether the system is helping or harming; second, an operational
governance framework, with owners, system cards, usage policies, escalation procedures and review
processes, because embedding AI in core processes without it multiplies risk; third, governed data
infrastructure and a shared platform, so that further use cases are built on accessible, governed
data and reusable components instead of one-off integrations. (Section 17.9)

**6.** As AI takes over implementation, people practice the underlying skills less and can lose
them, so they become less able to verify AI output, to catch subtle errors, and to do the work when
the AI is unavailable or wrong, while their reviews become rubber stamps. Mitigations: design
workflows in which people make the key decisions and explain them, not just approve output; require
reviewers to verify claims and code, not only read them; reserve some work, such as on-call
debugging, design problems and training exercises, for unassisted practice; rotate people through
tasks that keep core skills current; measure review quality, for example with seeded errors; and
calibrate trust by showing people where the AI has been wrong. Productivity is captured on routine
work, while judgment stays exercised. (Sections 17.4, 17.8)

## Chapter 18 — Final Capstone Project: Enterprise AI Platform

**1.** Deploy the platform separately in each region: an EU deployment in EU data centers and a US
deployment in US data centers, each with its own LLM gateway, RAG stores, vector databases, caches,
session stores and audit logs. Each tenant is assigned a home region recorded in its configuration.
The tenant router at the API gateway resolves the tenant from the authenticated token and routes the
request to its home region, rejecting cross-region routing for data-bearing requests; within the
EU deployment, model calls go to EU-region endpoints or self-hosted models, and no client data goes
to a third-party provider without consent. Audit logs are written in the tenant's home region to
immutable storage with 7-year retention. For US healthcare clients, HIPAA does not itself require US
residency, but the platform's requirement does, and HIPAA requires business associate agreements
with every provider that handles PHI, access controls and audit logging of PHI access. Only
non-personal operational metrics leave a region for global dashboards. (Sections 18.1, 18.2, 18.8;
Chapter 16, Section 16.10; Chapter 12, Section 12.6)

**2.** The client sends the request; the API gateway terminates TLS, validates the JWT through SSO,
applies rate limits, and the tenant router routes it to the tenant's region, while the audit logger
records receipt. The security layer runs prompt injection detection and PII handling. The agent
runtime receives the task: the goal decomposer and planner split it into retrieving documents,
querying the database and drafting the communication, and the context manager loads session state
and memory. For each step, the tool selector chooses a tool, the safety layer checks it against the
tenant's whitelist, and the executor runs it: the RAG service retrieves internal documents within the
tenant's access scope, and the database tool runs a scoped, read-only query. The LLM gateway, with
the prompt registry supplying the versioned template, routes the drafting call to a model, checking
the semantic cache first. The result evaluator checks the results, with retry or replanning on
failure. The output safety filter and PII scanner check the draft; because a client communication
is a client-affecting action, it goes to human-in-the-loop approval before it is sent. The cost
tracker records token usage, the evaluation pipeline may sample the response, the audit logger
records every step, and the response is returned to the user. (Sections 18.3, 18.6–18.8, Figures
18.1, 18.2)

**3.** Effort figures are rough estimates for planning, not measurements. (a) No bias evaluation of
the patient risk model, a MEASURE gap: define the relevant groups and fairness metrics with clinical
and legal input, build a representative labeled evaluation set, run disaggregated evaluation, add it
to the evaluation pipeline as a gate on every model change, and document results in the model card;
roughly two to six weeks, depending on data availability. (b) Audit log retention of 90 days instead of
7 years: change the retention policy on immutable storage, with tiered archive storage for older logs,
verify integrity mechanisms and access controls, and test retrieval; days to two weeks of engineering,
plus the storage cost; note that logs already deleted cannot be recovered, so record the gap. (c) No
designated AI officer, a GOVERN gap: an organizational remediation, in which leadership appoints an
accountable owner with a written mandate, authority and reporting line, and assigns governance
responsibilities; a few weeks of organizational work, not engineering. Then re-run the compliance
evaluation. (Sections 18.2, 18.7; Chapter 12, Sections 12.4, 12.8)

**4.** Controls that should have prevented it: tenant isolation in the RAG service and the tenant
router, so retrieval for a tenant-A session can only access tenant A's index, enforced in the
retrieval layer by the authenticated tenant identity, not by anything in the prompt; tool
whitelisting and scoped credentials, so the agent's tools cannot reach tenant B's stores at all;
prompt injection detection on inputs and retrieved content; output filtering and anomaly detection
for content from another tenant; per-tenant cache keys; and audit logs. Since tenant B's documents
were retrieved, the isolation enforced in the data layer failed or did not exist: retrieval or a
tool accepted a tenant identifier the model could influence, or used a shared index filtered only
by metadata the injection could alter, or a cache was shared across tenants. Required changes:
physically or logically separate per-tenant indexes and caches; derive the tenant scope only from the
authenticated session, passed to tools out of band; give each tenant's agent credentials that cannot
access other tenants' data; add a cross-tenant check on every retrieved document and output; and add
tests that attempt cross-tenant access. Treat it as a data breach: notify affected parties under the
applicable obligations. (Sections 18.6–18.8; Chapter 9; Chapter 10)

**5.** (a) Moving GPT-6.1 Sol tasks to GPT-6 Luna: 60% of $45,000 is $27,000; at Chapter 15's prices,
GPT-6 Luna costs 5% of GPT-6.1 Sol for both input and output tokens, so those tasks would cost $1,350,
saving $25,650. (b) Raising the cache hit rate from 20% to 40%: requests reaching the model fall from
80% to 60%, a 25% reduction in model spend, saving $11,250, assuming cached and uncached requests
cost the same on average. (c) Trimming over-provisioned summary context: 30% of $6,750 saves $2,025.
The sum is $38,925, but applied together the savings compound on a shrinking base: assuming the
summary tasks are not among those moved to the cheaper model, (a) leaves $19,350; (c) leaves $17,325;
and the cache then saves 25% of that, leaving $12,994. The combined saving is about $32,000 a month,
about 71%, less than the sum because each optimization reduces the base on which the others act.
Every saving must be confirmed with the evaluation suite. (Section 18.7; Chapter 15, Sections 15.2,
15.6, 15.7)

**6.** Build on the three tiers: automated safety checks on all traffic, LLM-as-judge on a sample of
about 10%, and expert human evaluation of a small sample focused on flagged cases and judge
calibration, with per-use-case evaluation sets versioned with the models and prompts, run on every
change as a quality gate and weekly on schedule. Metrics per use case: document analysis, extraction
accuracy against labeled fields and factual consistency of summaries with the source; agent tasks,
task completion by outcome verification, step efficiency and tool-use accuracy on mocked tools;
customer communication, judge-scored accuracy, tone and policy compliance, plus the approval and
edit rate from human reviewers; knowledge retrieval, context recall and precision, faithfulness and
answer relevance; code generation, unit-test pass rate, static analysis and security scanning.
Report per tenant and per use case, gate on each slice and not only the average, alert on sustained
drops in both short and long windows, and recalibrate the judges against human ratings monthly.
(Section 18.9; Chapter 14; Volume III, Chapters 4 and 17)
